claim: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
source_text: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
evidence_reasoning: This statement draws from established scientific understanding about microbial community function.

claim: In strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other.
source_text: We found that in strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental observations and simulations presented in the manuscript, as well as logical inference from the results.

claim: Partner intermixing in strong cooperation is insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
source_text: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing intermixing under various initial conditions (Figure 2-figure supplement 3A, Figure 3A, and Figure 3-figure supplement 1D).

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges.
source_text: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
source_text: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges and a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental observations of D. vulgaris and M. maripaludis biofilms (Figure 4).

claim: In simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
source_text: Even in simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 5.

claim: When ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
source_text: Thus, when ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is inferred from the combined experimental and simulation data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
source_text: However, understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established scientific understanding about the complexity of natural microbial communities.

claim: In a synthetic community, three bacterial species can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance.
source_text: in a synthetic community, three bacterial species, each contributing an essential benefit while simultaneously competing for these benefits, can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance (Kim et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth.
source_text: different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth (Christensen et al., 2002; Brenner and Arnold, 2011)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2002 and Brenner and Arnold, 2011.

claim: Branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface.
source_text: branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface (Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004.

claim: In waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates.
source_text: in waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates (Satoh et al., 2007)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Satoh et al., 2007.

claim: It is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community.
source_text: Thus, it is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community (Christensen et al., 2002; Wilmes et al., 2008; Dekas et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing pattern variability.

claim: Strong cooperation is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling to pathogenic biofilms.
source_text: This is because 1) it is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling (Schink, 2002; Falkowski et al., 2008; McInerney et al., 2009) to pathogenic biofilms (Kelly, 1980; Kolenbrander et al., 2010; Elias and Banin, 2012)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple citations and reflects established knowledge about microbial communities.

claim: The codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells.
source_text: 2) the codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells (Schink, 2002; McInerney et al., 2009)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations and reflects known challenges in microbiology.

claim: Cells initially divided and pushed other cells to the side such that all cells remained in the same plane.
source_text: Starting from one budding cell (a, hour 0.5), cells initially divided and pushed other cells to the side such that all cells remained in the same plane (b, hour 9).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on direct experimental observation of yeast cell growth (Figure 1-figure supplement 1A, Video 1).

claim: When the group of cells reached approximately 5-cell radius, cells in the center could no longer push other cells to the side and instead budded upward.
source_text: When the group of cells reached approximately 5-cell radius (c, hour 14), cells in the center could no longer push other cells to the side and instead budded upward, as indicated by higher intensities in the fluorescence images.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on direct experimental observation of yeast cell growth patterns.

claim: Interactions conferring large benefit to at least one partner could lead to ratio convergence.
source_text: The fitness model demonstrated that interactions conferring large benefit to at least one partner could lead to ratio convergence.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model (Figure 1-figure supplement 2).

claim: If two partner populations inhibit each other sufficiently strongly compared to their basal fitness, population ratios may diverge rapidly.
source_text: The fitness model shows that if two partner populations inhibit each other sufficiently strongly compared to their basal fitness, population ratios may diverge rapidly.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model (Figure 1-figure supplement 3).

claim: In [∼ ∼], [∼ ↓], and [↓ ↓], red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other.
source_text: In [∼ ∼], [∼ ↓], and [↓ ↓], red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other (Figure 1C–E).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on simulation results showing segregated patterns in these interaction types.

claim: In [↑ ↓] and [∼ ↑], frequently one of the populations either formed a column or became covered by the partner population.
source_text: In [↑ ↓] and [∼ ↑], frequently one of the populations (green) either formed a column or became covered by the partner population (red) (Figure 1F–G).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on simulation results showing layered patterns in these interaction types.

claim: Only in cooperation conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively intermixed.
source_text: Only in cooperation ([↑ ↑]) conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively 'intermixed', manifested as the two different cell types successively piling on top of each other (Figure 1H).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on simulation results showing intermixed patterns specifically in strong cooperation.

claim: Statistically significant differences in intermixing indexes were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions.
source_text: Statistically significant differences were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions (Figure 1I).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by statistical analysis of simulation results (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.01).

claim: Population ratios converged in the commensal and cooperative but not competitive communities.
source_text: Using engineered competitive, obligatory commensal, and obligatory cooperative yeast communities (see below), we confirmed that population ratios converged in the commensal and cooperative but not competitive communities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on experimental measurements using flow cytometry in engineered yeast communities.

claim: Convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply.
source_text: This convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply (Shou et al., 2007)
evidence_reasoning: This interpretation is supported by a citation and logical inference from the observed convergence.

claim: If the supplier population suddenly increased in relative abundance, then each individual in the consumer population would receive more benefit and grow faster, which would return the ratio to its original value.
source_text: if, for instance, the supplier population suddenly increased in relative abundance, then each individual in the consumer population would receive more benefit and grow faster, which would return the ratio to its original value.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference explaining the mechanism of ratio convergence.

claim: In obligatory commensal communities, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers.
source_text: In obligatory commensal communities, since one supplier could support the birth of multiple consumers, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers (top-views in B and vertical cross-sections in E).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations and simulations of commensal yeast communities.

claim: Obligatory cooperative communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views and patchy cross-section patterns.
source_text: Obligatory cooperative communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views (C, 6× magnification insets in experiments) and patchy cross-section patterns (F).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations and simulations of cooperative yeast communities.

claim: The intermixing index increased linearly with community height in obligatory cooperative communities.
source_text: In contrast, the intermixing index in obligatory cooperative communities increased proportionally to community height in both experiments and the diffusion model (Figure 2G, magenta).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by quantitative analysis of both experimental and simulation data.

claim: A characteristic patch size of 10–20 µm was observed in cooperative communities.
source_text: This proportionality suggested the existence of a characteristic patch size ('Spatial analysis' in 'Materials and methods'), denoted λz*, of 10–20 µm.
evidence_reasoning: This is derived from quantitative analysis of experimental cooperative communities.

claim: The characteristic patch size was independent of initial conditions.
source_text: The characteristic patch size was independent of initial conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing consistent patch sizes across different initial conditions.

claim: A calculation of the patch size based on experimentally-determined release, diffusion, and consumption of exchanged metabolites yielded comparable results to observed patch sizes.
source_text: Indeed, a calculation of the patch size based on experimentally-determined release, diffusion, and consumption of exchanged metabolites yielded comparable results ('Calculating the characteristic patch size in cooperative yeast communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence_reasoning: This is based on theoretical calculations using experimentally measured parameters.

claim: If cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished.
source_text: Using the diffusion model, we found that if cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results testing different distribution scenarios.

claim: Local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to take turns to grow, which leads to population intermixing.
source_text: Based on this result and based on patterns observed in top-views and vertical cross-sections of cooperative communities, we propose that local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to 'take turns' to grow, which leads to population intermixing (Figure 2H).
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from experimental observations and simulation results.

claim: Intermixing was insensitive to initial conditions in yeast obligatory cooperative communities.
source_text: We found that intermixing was insensitive to initial conditions in the yeast obligatory cooperative communities.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data testing various initial population ratios and densities.

claim: Edge sections of obligatory cooperative communities showed significantly more intermixing than those from non-cooperative communities.
source_text: even though both obligatory cooperative and non-cooperative communities directly above the high-density inoculation spot showed high population intermixing ('Center'), edge sections ('Edge') of obligatory cooperative communities showed significantly more intermixing than those from non-cooperative communities (Mann–Whitney U test, p<5 × 10−5).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis comparing cooperative and non-cooperative communities.

claim: Facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits required greater community heights to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
source_text: In simulations using the fitness model, facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits required greater community heights to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model (Figure 3B).

claim: Partner intermixing is insensitive to diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm²/s.
source_text: In the diffusion model, obligatory cooperative communities with diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm2/s (corresponding to the diffusion constants of Sulforhodamine 101 in yeast community and agarose, respectively) both showed significant partner intermixing during growth.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results testing different diffusion constants (Figure 3-figure supplement 1A).

claim: Intermixing does not depend on asymmetry between cooperating partners.
source_text: We examined symmetric obligatory cooperation by assuming that for the two partners, all live cells released nutrients at a constant and identical rate without delay, and that other properties such as rates of growth, death, and nutrient consumption were also identical. Partner intermixing in this symmetric obligatory cooperative system (Sym. coop) was similar to that in asymmetric obligatory yeast cooperative system (Coop).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results comparing symmetric and asymmetric cooperation (Figure 3-figure supplement 1C).

claim: Desulfovibrio vulgaris and Methanococcus maripaludis cooperate through redox coupling.
source_text: In the absence of sulfate and hydrogen, the bacterium Desulfovibrio vulgaris (Dv) and the archaeon Methanococcus maripaludis (Mm) cooperate through redox coupling.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established knowledge about these organisms' metabolic interactions.

claim: D. vulgaris ferments lactate and produces mainly acetate, CO2, and H2, but this reaction is not thermodynamically favorable unless H2 is kept at very low concentrations.
source_text: Dv ferments lactate and produces mainly acetate, CO2, and H2. However, this reaction is not thermodynamically favorable unless H2 is kept at very low concentrations.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established biochemical knowledge about D. vulgaris metabolism.

claim: H2 produced by D. vulgaris is used by M. maripaludis to reduce CO2 to methane.
source_text: H2 is used by Mm to reduce CO2 to methane.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established knowledge about M. maripaludis metabolism.

claim: In cooperative biofilms of D. vulgaris and M. maripaludis, the intermixing index increased with height.
source_text: In cooperative biofilms of Dv (green) and Mm (red), the intermixing index increased with height.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations using FISH analysis of biofilm cross-sections (Figure 4B).

claim: Naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
source_text: Thus, naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental observations of D. vulgaris-M. maripaludis biofilms.

claim: Most of the cooperative pairs intermixed in simulated multi-species communities.
source_text: Quantifying intermixing in a total of 240 interactions from 24 independent communities showed that most of the cooperative pairs intermixed (magenta).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation results from multi-species communities (Figure 5D).

claim: Indirect interactions through other community members could make cooperative pairs not intermixed or non-cooperative pairs intermixed.
source_text: Indirect interactions through other community members could make cooperative pairs not intermixed (grey) or non-cooperative (commensal) pairs intermixed (brown).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results showing exceptions to the general pattern (Figure 5D).

claim: Interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner can potentially result in ratio convergence.
source_text: The first expectation is that interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner ([↑ ↑], [∼ ↑], and [↓ ↑]) can potentially result in ratio convergence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by both simulation and experimental results, as well as analytical calculations.

claim: In [↑ ↑] and [∼ ↑], global stability can be achieved whereas in [↓ ↑], local stability can be achieved.
source_text: An analytical calculation based on the fitness model showed that in [↑ ↑] and [∼ ↑], global stability can be achieved whereas in [↓ ↑], local stability can be achieved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; 'Requirements for steady-state ratios in the six types of communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence_reasoning: This is based on analytical calculations derived from the fitness model.

claim: In competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value.
source_text: In contrast, in competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value which will remain unchanged until the next perturbation.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference from the properties of equal-fitness competition.

claim: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
source_text: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference from the properties of unequal-fitness competition.

claim: Strong cooperation results in partner intermixing in the direction vertical to the surface of initial colonization.
source_text: The second expectation is that strong cooperation results in partner intermixing in the direction vertical to the surface of initial colonization.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple experimental and simulation results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cooperative intermixing requires spatially localized benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners.
source_text: Cooperative intermixing requires spatially localized benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3B)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results testing different benefit localization scenarios.

claim: Cooperative intermixing is robust against variations in initial conditions or reaction dynamics.
source_text: and otherwise appears to be robust against variations in initial conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) or reaction dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental and simulation results testing various conditions.

claim: The intermixing indexes in cooperative communities increased linearly as a function of community height because these communities exhibited fixed-size patches associated with the spatial localization of benefits.
source_text: The intermixing indexes in these communities increased linearly as a function of community height, because these communities exhibited fixed-size patches associated with the spatial localization of benefits
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference based on quantitative analysis of experimental and simulation data.

claim: In a theoretical study using a one-dimensional stepping-stone model, strongly cooperating partners also appeared much more mixed than competing partners.
source_text: In a theoretical study using a one-dimensional stepping-stone model, strongly cooperating partners also appeared much more mixed than competing partners (Korolev and Nelson, 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Korolev and Nelson, 2011.

claim: Competing bacterial species form a columnar or layered pattern.
source_text: For instance, competing bacterial species form a columnar or layered pattern (Palmer et al., 2001; Kreth et al., 2005; An et al., 2006; Hallatschek et al., 2007; Bernstein et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies showing segregated patterns in competing species.

claim: Burkholderia sp. LB400 and Pseudomonas sp. B13(FR1) show spatial segregation as competitors when grown on citrate, but when grown on chlorobiphenyl they engage in metabolic commensalism and exhibit a layered pattern.
source_text: Burkholderia sp. LB400 and Pseudomonas sp. B13(FR1) show spatial segregation as competitors when grown on citrate, but when grown on chlorobiphenyl they engage in metabolic commensalism and exhibit a layered pattern (Nielsen et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2000.

claim: When grown on a non-selective carbon source, Comamonas testosteroni WDL7 outcompeted and covered Variovorax sp. WDL1, but when fed with an aromatic compound as the sole carbon source, competition switched to cooperation and the two populations intermixed.
source_text: Similarly, when grown on a non-selective carbon source, Comamonas testosteroni WDL7 outcompeted and covered Variovorax sp. WDL1, but when fed with an aromatic compound as the sole carbon source, competition switched to cooperation and the two populations intermixed (Breugelmans et al., 2008).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Breugelmans et al., 2008.

claim: Cooperative oral bacteria species intermixed when grown on saliva.
source_text: Cooperative oral bacteria species intermixed when grown on saliva (Palmer et al., 2001; Periasamy and Kolenbrander, 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 2001 and Periasamy and Kolenbrander, 2009.

claim: If at least one population actively moves or grows hyphae to penetrate the entire community, two populations might appear intermixed even if they do not cooperate.
source_text: However, it is conceivable that if at least one population actively moves (Houry et al., 2012) or grows hyphae to penetrate the entire community, two populations might appear intermixed even if they do not cooperate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about potential deviations from expected patterns, with a citation supporting the possibility of active movement.

claim: In biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two populations differing only in fluorescent colors showed modest intermixing even though the expectation for equal-fitness competition is a columnar pattern.
source_text: In biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two populations differing only in fluorescent colors (Klausen et al., 2003) showed modest intermixing even though the expectation for equal-fitness competition is a columnar pattern with an intermixing index close to zero (Figure 2D, left).
evidence_reasoning: This observation is supported by a citation and represents a deviation from the expected pattern.

claim: The modest intermixing in P. aeruginosa biofilms was caused by P. aeruginosa differentiating into non-motile 'stalk' cells that anchored to the surface and motile cells that climbed up to form the mushroom-like caps.
source_text: This modest intermixing was caused by P. aeruginosa differentiating into non-motile 'stalk' cells that anchored to the surface and motile cells that climbed up to form the mushroom-like caps (Klausen et al., 2003).
evidence_reasoning: This mechanistic explanation is supported by a citation to Klausen et al., 2003.

claim: If two cooperating populations have very different preferences for oxygen, then the two populations are likely not to intermix and instead form layers.
source_text: For instance, if two cooperating populations have very different preferences for oxygen, then the two populations are likely not to intermix and instead form layers in which the aerobic population is exposed to oxygen while the anaerobic population is protected from oxygen.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about how environmental factors could alter expected patterns.

claim: Variability in patterning has been observed within and between communities, even if they were grown in laboratory-controlled environments.
source_text: Variability in patterning has been observed within and between communities (Christensen et al., 2002; Wilmes et al., 2008; Dekas et al., 2009), even if they were grown in laboratory-controlled environments (Christensen et al., 2002).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting pattern variability.

claim: Stochastic events such as environmental variability, mutations, or fluctuations in initial conditions can all lead to variable patterns.
source_text: Stochastic events such as environmental variability, mutations, or fluctuations in initial conditions can all lead to variable patterns.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about potential sources of pattern variability.

claim: For mutually antagonistic interactions, population ratios can quickly diverge, and which population eventually dominates depends on the initial population ratio.
source_text: For mutually antagonistic interactions, the fitness model showed that population ratios can quickly diverge. Thus, which population eventually dominates depends on the initial population ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by simulation results from the fitness model.

claim: Different patterns have been observed for communities formed by two antagonistic bacteria species.
source_text: Indeed, different patterns have been observed for communities formed by two antagonistic bacteria species (Kuramitsu et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by a citation to Kuramitsu et al., 2007.
